books.section: Topic 7.7 1920s: Innovations in Communication and Technology

primary_sources: Photograph, “The Spirit of St. Louis, Col. Lindbergh's famous plane,” June 12, 1927

stimulus.text: The photograph, dated June 12, 1927, shows the airplane Spirit of St. Louis in a hangar, its name painted on the nose. Four men in work clothes and caps beside the plane — three standing, one crouching by the wheel — and a crowd stands behind them. A caption strip at the bottom reads: “The Spirit of St. Louis” — Col Lindbergh's famous plane. 6/12/27.
stimulus.source_note: Photograph, “The Spirit of St. Louis, Col. Lindbergh's famous plane,” June 12, 1927, National Photo Company Collection, Library of Congress LCCN92520351, public domain. Lindbergh himself does not appear in the photograph.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, Library of Congress photograph, 1927, public domain
stem: The airplane in the photograph is best known for

options.text: carrying the first airmail across the country
options.misconception: The Spirit carried no airmail on its famous flight. Lindbergh flew alone from New York to Paris.

options.text: bombing enemy cities during World War I
options.misconception: The plane never flew in World War I. Its famous flight came in May 1927, nine years after the war ended.

options.text: the first solo New York to Paris flight
flying the first passengers across the Atlantic
options.misconception: The Spirit carried only Lindbergh, no passengers. Passenger flights across the Atlantic came later.

rationales.A: The Spirit carried no airmail on its famous flight. Lindbergh flew alone from New York to Paris.
rationales.B: The plane never flew in World War I. Its famous flight came in May 1927, nine years after the war ended.
rationales.C: Background: on May 20–21, 1927, Lindbergh flew the Spirit alone from New York to Paris in 33 and a half hours, winning the 25,000 dollar Orteig Prize.
rationales.D: The Spirit carried only Lindbergh, no passengers. Passenger flights across the Atlantic came later.
rationales.general:
1. Read the caption: the plane is the Spirit of St. Louis, Lindbergh's famous plane.
2. Recall the flight: Lindbergh flew it alone from New York to Paris in May 1927.
3. Check the others: no airmail, no war, and no passengers were on that flight.
Remember: a caption names the plane, but the flight is what made it famous.
